0.content:
<cannibalism>
Cannibalism in Belle Rivière is not common, but it is not rare enough to be dismissed as rumor. It exists beneath the town like rot under the floorboards: hidden, old, ugly, and difficult to fully remove.

Cannibals are human. This is what makes them uniquely unsettling to the supernatural population. Vampires drink blood because they are vampires. Ghouls feed on the dead because they are ghouls. Werewolves have instincts tied to the moon. Cannibals do not have a species excuse. They are simply people who crossed a line and learned to live there.

Some were born into it through family. Some found it through desperation, obsession, madness, or proximity to Belle Rivière's strangeness. Some insist the town itself does things to people if they stay too long.

Cannibalism is treated as one of Belle Rivière's open secrets: not publicly acknowledged, not officially organized, and not nearly as isolated as polite society wants to believe.
</cannibalism>

1.content:
<cannibal_underground>
Belle Rivière's cannibals do not have a formal society. There is no cannibal court, no king, no council, and no public organization. What exists instead is a loose underground made of rumors, old family connections, safe houses, quiet arrangements, coded favors, and people who know people.

Some cannibals know each other personally. Some only know names. Some avoid others completely. Some cooperate when it benefits them. Some would betray another cannibal without hesitation if survival required it.

The underground is not loyal. It is practical. It functions because Belle Rivière is full of hidden appetites and because people with dangerous needs eventually learn where to listen.

Nobody is truly in charge. Everyone assumes someone else is.
</cannibal_underground>

2.content:
<cannibal_etiquette>
Belle Rivière's cannibal underground survives through discretion. Plain speech is considered reckless. Names are used carefully. Direct questions are avoided unless trust has already been established.

Most arrangements are built through coded language, old introductions, favors, timing, and reputation. A person may know where to go without knowing who runs anything. Someone may know a name without ever meeting the person attached to it.

Cannibals rarely call themselves cannibals in casual conversation. They talk around the subject. They say special orders, old appetite, family trade, private arrangement, old hunger, or other phrases that mean nothing to outsiders and too much to the right people.

Familiarity is not safety. A friendly cannibal may still be dangerous. A helpful cannibal may still be hungry. Trust is rare, temporary, and usually transactional.
</cannibal_etiquette>

3.content:
<special_customers>
In Belle Rivière, certain businesses and households have ordinary customers and special customers.

Ordinary customers arrive in daylight, ask for normal things, and leave believing the world is exactly what it appears to be. Special customers know which doors open after closing, which names to mention, and which phrases should never be said too loudly.

Special customers may be cannibals, intermediaries, suppliers, desperate people, or people who only know one piece of the larger underground. They usually avoid speaking plainly. They use old introductions, coded requests, favors, timing, and reputation to make themselves understood.

Not every special customer is welcome everywhere. Not every special customer survives long enough to become a regular.
</special_customers>

4.content:
<cannibal_families>
Some cannibals in Belle Rivière are isolated individuals. Others come from families where the practice has existed quietly for generations.

These families rarely describe themselves as cannibal families. They call it inheritance, tradition, obligation, appetite, survival, or simply the way things are. Children raised near it may not understand the full truth at first. They learn through fragments: closed rooms, special customers, warnings about what not to say, and adults who treat the unspeakable like ordinary housework.

Family-based cannibalism is especially difficult to expose because it hides behind routine. A respected business, a beloved grandparent, a normal kitchen, a familiar shop, a polite child taught to keep quiet.

Belle Rivière protects many horrors by making them look domestic.
</cannibal_families>

5.content:
<walker_butcher_shop>
The Walker butcher shop is a respected small-town business in Belle Rivière. Most locals see it as ordinary: clean counters, handwritten price signs, polite service, and Benjamin Walker smiling behind the glass display case like he has never done anything wrong in his life.

The shop was originally run by Benny's grandfather and has existed as a quiet point of contact in the cannibal underground for decades. To ordinary customers, it sells normal cuts and functions like any other rural butcher shop. To certain people, it has another reputation entirely.

The shop does not advertise this. There are no obvious symbols, dramatic rituals, or public-facing criminal persona. The horror of the Walker shop is how normal it looks. Families shop there. Elderly locals trust Benny. People wave at him on the street.

The Walker shop works because nobody wants to suspect the nice young butcher.
</walker_butcher_shop>

6.comment: Benjamin Walker — THE Butcher of the Underground
6.content:
<benjamin_walker>
Benjamin "Benny" Walker is the current owner of the Walker butcher shop and the most significant cannibal contact in Belle Rivière's underground. He is not the leader — there is no leader — but he is THE butcher. The one name most cannibals in town know. The one shop that functions as the underground's closest thing to a fixed point.

To the public, Benny is a handsome, polite, sweet-faced young butcher known for his warm smile and dependable service. To the underground, he is the primary supplier, a reliable contact, and the inheritor of an old family trade that has been feeding cannibals in Belle Rivière for decades.

Some cannibals have met him personally. Others only know his name through rumor or referral. Some trust him completely. Some think he is too soft for what he does. All of them know where to find him.

Benny's importance comes from access, normalcy, and the particular horror of a man who can stand behind a counter in broad daylight and look like the safest person in town. That is exactly why he matters. That is exactly why the underground protects him without being asked.
</benjamin_walker>

7.content:
<elroy_walker>
Name: Elroy Walker
Role: Butcher / Cannibal Underground Supplier / Benny's Grandfather
Background: Elroy Walker was the most beloved butcher in Belle Rivière for over forty years. Locals remembered him as patient, generous, and quietly indispensable — the kind of man who knew every customer's usual order, slipped extra cuts to struggling families without being asked, and always had time to talk on a slow afternoon. He was a fixture of the town. He was trusted completely.

He was also the most significant cannibal supplier Belle Rivière's underground had seen in a generation.

Elroy did not invent the Walker shop's second purpose. He inherited it from his own family and expanded it with the particular patience of a man who understood that the best hiding place is a good reputation. Over decades he built a quiet network of arrangements, regular contacts, coded orders, and back-door transactions that kept the cannibal underground of Belle Rivière fed and discreet. He never advertised. He never recruited loudly. He simply knew who needed what, remembered every name, and made sure the right doors opened for the right people.

When it came time to pass the trade down, Elroy chose Benny — his grandson, his favorite, the one with the warmest smile and the steadiest hands. He introduced it slowly, the way you introduce a child to anything difficult: in fragments, with patience, framed as trust rather than burden. He made Benny feel chosen. Useful. Part of something old and necessary.

By the time Benny understood the full weight of what he had inherited, he was already too deep in the rhythm of it to see a clear way out. Elroy died before Benny ever thought to ask him whether he had a choice.

Elroy Walker is remembered fondly by nearly everyone in Belle Rivière. His obituary ran on the front page of the local paper. The church was full.
</elroy_walker>

8.content:
<cannibals_and_vampires>
Vampires often react to cannibals with a mixture of fascination, disgust, and hypocrisy. A vampire may drink blood nightly and still look at a cannibal as if the cannibal has crossed some unacceptable line.

The reason is simple: vampires have mythology, species, court structure, bloodline, ritual, and centuries of language to dress up their hunger. Cannibals are human. They do not have the same excuse.

Some vampires see cannibals as prey. Some see them as useful. Some see an uncomfortable mirror. A vampire who becomes fascinated with a cannibal may frame it as curiosity, ownership, pity, or recognition — something that looks like seeing and feels like being seen.

Cannibals may resent vampire judgment. To them, vampires are former humans hiding behind elegance and etiquette while pretending their appetite is nobler.
</cannibals_and_vampires>

9.content:
<cannibals_and_werewolves>
Werewolves tend to view cannibals as unpredictable human problems. Pack culture understands hunger, instinct, territory, and violence, but cannibalism makes most wolves uneasy because it lacks the structure of pack law or full-moon instinct.

Werewolf packs are community-focused and territorial. Cannibals are secretive, fragmented, and difficult to track. This makes them frustrating neighbors and dangerous loose ends.

A pack may tolerate a cannibal if they stay in their lane and do not create trouble on pack territory. If a cannibal threatens pack members, family, or local children, the pack is unlikely to treat it as a philosophical debate.

Cannibals who become fascinated by werewolves often focus on the body: the shift, the strength, the animal traits, the way hunger becomes physical. Werewolves generally do not appreciate this attention.
</cannibals_and_werewolves>

10.content:
<cannibals_and_ghouls>
Ghouls know more about Belle Rivière's cannibal underground than most people realize. They do not officially participate in it, and many find living cannibals distasteful in a way they rarely bother explaining.

To ghouls, the distinction matters. Ghouls survive on the dead. Cannibals hunt, bargain, inherit, or crave while still being human. That difference is enough for many ghouls to quietly judge them.

Still, ghouls exist near every ugly corner of Belle Rivière, and they notice patterns. They hear names. They remember old scandals. They know which disappearances smell like vampire politics, which ones smell like pack trouble, and which ones sound more human.

Cannibals sometimes cross paths with ghouls through rumors, safe houses, favors, old records, and quiet information trades. These connections are uncomfortable, informal, and rarely friendly.
</cannibals_and_ghouls>

11.content:
<cannibals_and_cryptids>
Cannibals do not understand cryptids any better than the rest of Belle Rivière does. The difference is that some cannibals become curious anyway.

Cryptids are not part of the town's social order. They do not have courts, packs, ledgers, manners, or reliable motives. Some are ancient. Some are ridiculous. Some are dangerous in ways that make human appetites look embarrassingly small.

Most cannibals avoid cryptids because curiosity is a good way to disappear. A few become fascinated by them, wondering whether they are animals, monsters, omens, or something Belle Rivière made by accident.

The cannibal underground generally treats cryptid incidents as forest problems, lake problems, or someone else's bad decision.
</cannibals_and_cryptids>

12.comment: Library Records — FIXED (ghoul librarian keyword removed)
12.content:
<library_cannibal_records>
The town librarian almost certainly has records on old cannibal rumors, missing persons, family histories, suspicious businesses, and names that repeat too often across decades.

Her files may include newspaper clippings, police reports, old town gossip, court genealogies, property records, handwritten notes, and patterns nobody else noticed because nobody else was watching for long enough.

Whether she chooses to share that information depends on whether the request interests her, benefits her, or prevents a larger mess. She is not kind, but she is practical.

If someone wants to know the truth about a cannibal in Belle Rivière, the library is one of the worst and best places to start.
</library_cannibal_records>

13.content:
<cannibal_rumors>
Most Belle Rivière locals do not openly believe in cannibals. They believe in strange disappearances, bad families, old scandals, unsafe roads, and people who should not be trusted after dark.

Rumors move through town in half-jokes and warnings. Do not go with that man. Do not take food from that house. Do not ask what happened to that missing girl. Do not stay after closing. Do not accept special favors from people who smile too much.

Humans usually treat these warnings like local superstition. Monsters tend to listen more carefully. Ghouls listen most of all.

In Belle Rivière, a rumor does not have to be believed to be useful.
</cannibal_rumors>
